stemMd:
Early readers valued the physician's diary of the epidemic above the official reports precisely because they took it to be **(i)** ______. The discovery of a fair copy, corrected in his hand and addressed to a printer, has made that assumption difficult to **(ii)** ______: a man preparing his journal for an audience had every reason to **(iii)** ______ his own conduct during the crisis, and the entries in which he appears most selfless are, tellingly, the ones he revised most heavily.

**Blank (i):** unguarded / comprehensive / elegant

**Blank (ii):** sustain / dispute / isolate

**Blank (iii):** burnish / record / forget
instructionsMd: Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices. All blanks must be correct; there is no credit for a partially correct answer.
explanationMd:
The first blank is the hardest to fill on its own: readers might value a diary for many reasons. Leave it open, and let the rest of the passage tell you which reason the discovery undermined.

**Blank (iii) first — it has the fullest evidence.** The final clause says the entries in which the physician "appears most selfless" are "the ones he revised most heavily." Heavy revision concentrated on the flattering passages means he was improving his own image. **"Burnish"** (to polish, to make something look better) is that motive.

**Blank (ii) next — the colon.** The colon introduces the reason the fair copy damages the earlier view: a man writing for an audience had every reason to polish his own conduct. That is an argument *against* the early readers' assumption, so the discovery has made the assumption difficult to keep holding. **"Sustain"** fits.

**Blank (i) last — what did the discovery undermine?** The argument after the colon attacks one thing only: the idea that the diary was written without regard to how its author would look. So what early readers prized, and what the fair copy calls into doubt, is that the diary was private and off its guard. **"Unguarded"** is that quality. **The answer is unguarded, sustain and burnish.**

**How to check.** Read the whole passage through and ask whether the colon's evidence attacks exactly the quality in blank (i). With *unguarded*, it does: a writer preparing for readers is on his guard. With either of the other first-blank words, the evidence after the colon would be aimed at something the early readers never claimed, and the passage would stop making one argument.

distractorRationale.blank1-c: "Comprehensive" means complete in scope. A reader could value a diary for its completeness, but the evidence after the colon concerns a motive to flatter himself, which says nothing about how much the diary covers, so the discovery would not make a belief in its completeness hard to hold.
distractorRationale.blank1-b: "Elegant" is tempting because a manuscript addressed to a printer suggests polish. But a fair copy prepared for publication would, if anything, support a belief in the diary's elegance rather than undermine it, and the passage says the discovery undermined the early readers' assumption.
distractorRationale.blank2-c: "Dispute" reverses the logic. The evidence after the colon (a motive to flatter himself, and heavy revision of the flattering entries) counts against the early readers' assumption, so the discovery makes that assumption hard to keep, not hard to challenge.
distractorRationale.blank2-b: "Isolate" does not fit the argument. The evidence after the colon bears on whether the assumption is true, and nothing in the passage concerns separating the assumption from anything else.
distractorRationale.blank3-a: "Record" is the weak version of the answer. Any diarist records his conduct; that motive would not make the diary less trustworthy, and it does not explain why revision was concentrated on the entries that make him look most selfless.
distractorRationale.blank3-c: "Forget" is the opposite of what the final clause shows. A man who heavily revised the entries about his own selflessness was dwelling on his conduct, not trying to put it out of mind.

accessibilityText: A passage with three blanks. Early readers valued the physician's diary of the epidemic above the official reports precisely because they took it to be blank one. The discovery of a fair copy, corrected in his hand and addressed to a printer, has made that assumption difficult to blank two, colon, a man preparing his journal for an audience had every reason to blank three his own conduct during the crisis, and the entries in which he appears most selfless are, tellingly, the ones he revised most heavily. For blank one choose among unguarded, comprehensive and elegant. For blank two choose among sustain, dispute and isolate. For blank three choose among burnish, record and forget. All three blanks must be correct.

provenance.notes: Original three-blank Text Completion written for wave 7. The physician, his diary, the fair copy and the epidemic are invented. Unlike a blank fixed by apposition, blank (i) here has no local gloss: each of its three choices is a reason someone might value a diary, and only the argument completed by blanks (ii) and (iii) shows which quality the discovery undermines. Option ids carry blank1-, blank2- and blank3- prefixes matching the answer key's columnIds. Not adapted from any ETS item.

review.notes: Author solved as unguarded, sustain and burnish, twice. Stretch: harder than a typical hard three-blank item because the first blank has no gloss of its own and is fixed only by working backwards from the third blank and the final clause; a reader who fills the blanks in order must hold three open choices for the first blank until the end. Uniqueness: comprehensive is untouched by an argument about self-flattery; elegant would be supported, not undermined, by a fair copy for a printer; dispute reverses the direction of the evidence; isolate is off-topic; record does not explain revision concentrated on the flattering entries; forget contradicts heavy revision. Checked all twenty-seven combinations. Awaiting blind independent solve; the author must not publish own work. Options were reordered after review to remove answer-position bias; ids and labels were remapped with the key.
